opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it went better than I feared, but with some real lessons.

The bet was that we didn't have good ways to measure what AI agents could actually *do*. We had lots of multiple-choice benchmarks that were saturating, and they didn't tell you much about whether a system could carry out a long, messy, real-world task. So instead of spreading money across everything in AI safety evaluation, I wanted to go deep on one question: can we build benchmarks for agents doing difficult, consequential tasks, where the scores would mean something to policymakers and to the labs?

The narrow focus had real advantages. I could actually engage with each grantee. I could push on task design, on whether a benchmark would saturate too quickly, on whether the tasks reflected things people cared about, like doing real software engineering or AI research. That kind of hands-on shaping just isn't possible if you're running a broad program with a hundred grants and a skeleton crew.

The costs were also real. It's very time-intensive. Benchmarks take longer to build than people expect, and the field moves so fast that something you scoped a year ago can be half-obsolete when it ships. Some projects ended up measuring things that models blew past before the benchmark got much use. I also think I underweighted how much it matters to have elicitation done well. A benchmark is only as informative as the effort you put into getting the best performance out of the model. Otherwise you get false reassurance.

If I did it again, I'd keep the depth but build in more flexibility. I'd fund shorter iteration cycles, design tasks with much longer time horizons from the start, and invest more in the infrastructure for running agents properly. But I don't regret going narrow. In a space where nobody had a clear picture of agent capabilities, having a few really good measuring sticks was worth more than having many mediocre ones.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts focused funding with spreading money across AI safety evaluation, but it does not present the skeptical case that this focus foreclosed readily available funding opportunities in other areas.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's been a mixed bag, and I think it's worth being candid about that.

When I was leading the technical AI safety grantmaking at Open Phil, one of the bets we made was to put a lot of effort into a relatively narrow area: benchmarks that measure what AI agents can actually do in the world. The reasoning was that the biggest disagreements about AI risk and AI timelines often come down to empirical questions about capabilities, and the discourse was really starved for good measurements. If you could get a well-designed, hard-to-game benchmark for, say, long-horizon software engineering tasks or autonomous replication, you'd get something that feeds into forecasting, into lab safety policies, into government conversations, all at once. So I thought the leverage was high.

The high-effort part meant we weren't just writing checks. We were writing detailed RFPs, going back and forth with applicants on task design, pushing on things like contamination, scoring, whether the tasks actually reflected real-world difficulty. That was a lot of staff time per dollar moved, which is unusual for a funder.

Where I think it went well: some of the work that came out of that did become reference points that labs and evaluators actually use, and it helped build a small community of people who think carefully about evals as a discipline rather than a side project. I also think it sharpened my own views on how fast agentic capabilities were moving, because I was looking at the raw results closely.

Where I'd be more critical: narrow focus has costs. Benchmarks saturate fast, often faster than the grant cycle, so some of what we funded was outdated by the time it shipped. We were also sometimes slower than the labs themselves, who have far more compute and model access, so there's a real question about whether an external funder is the right actor for parts of this. And being this hands-on meant we probably underfunded other things, including some more exploratory, weirder work that doesn't fit cleanly into a benchmark frame.

So my overall assessment is that it was a reasonable bet given what we knew, it produced real value, but I'd weight it differently if I were doing it again. I'd keep some of the hands-on rigor but spend more of it on the infrastructure around evals, like who gets model access and how results get interpreted, rather than on individual task suites that have a short shelf life.

r001.rationale: The response says the narrow focus may have underfunded other work, including exploratory projects outside the benchmark frame. It does not communicate that readily available funding opportunities across other areas were foregone.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a bet with a pretty specific theory of change. We’re trying to fund benchmarks that tell us something important about what AI agents can actually do over longer tasks, where existing evaluations might not give us a clear picture. And doing that well can take a lot of work: you need good tasks, a credible way to score them, and some reason to think the results will matter for decisions people make.

The downside is that we could spend a lot of effort on a narrow slice of the problem and miss other valuable opportunities. So I wouldn’t assess the approach just by whether we produced a technically impressive benchmark. I’d ask: Did we learn something we otherwise wouldn’t have known? Did that change anyone’s understanding or behavior? And was the extra effort worth it relative to making more, smaller bets?

I’m sympathetic to going deep when there’s a real gap, but I’d want to stay willing to change course if the work isn’t producing that kind of value.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges that focusing effort narrowly could mean missing other valuable opportunities, but it does not clearly say this foregoes readily available funding opportunities across other areas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a bet worth making, but I’m pretty uncertain about it. The reason to put a lot of effort into a narrow set of benchmarks is that you can learn things you wouldn’t learn from a more superficial evaluation—especially about whether an agent can actually carry out a task over a long period, rather than just produce a convincing-looking answer.

The risk is that you end up with something very bespoke that doesn’t generalize, or that becomes obsolete as the models improve. So I’d judge the approach less by whether we produce a definitive score for AI agents and more by whether we uncover important failure modes and help people make better decisions about what these systems can reliably do.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty and notes risks that benchmarks may be bespoke or become obsolete, but it does not say that focusing grantmaking effort on them means forgoing readily available funding opportunities in other areas.
